obs: "and where the remedy is limited to a particular form of action, all the general incidents of that action must attach upon it."

"That act declares, that the mode of proceeding in civil causes in the courts of the United States in Louisiana, shall be conformable to the laws directing the mode of practice in the district courts of the states; with a power in the judge, to make rules to adapt such laws of-procedure to the organization of the courts of the United States."

"that court was required to proceed according to the principles, rules, and usages, which belong to courts of equity, as contra-distinguished from courts of law"; "There can, therefore, be no mistake in considering, that the whole system of English equity jurisprudence henceforth is the law of Louisiana, both in form and substance"

"that to effectuate the purposes of the legislature, the remedies in the Courts of the United States are to be at common law, or in equity, not according to the practice of the State Courts, but according to the principles of common law and equity as distinguished and defined in that country from which we derived our knowledge of those principles"

"In every instance in which this court has expounded the phrases, proceedings at the common law and proceedings in equity, with reference to the exercise of the judicial powers of the courts of the United States, they will be found to have interpreted the former as signifying the application of the definitions and principles and rules of the common law...; and the latter, as meaning the administration... of the equity law as defined and enforced by the Court of Chancery in England."
“But the case presented by the record is not a case at law, according to the meaning of those words, in courts which recognise the distinction between law and equity.”

"This makes it unnecessary to give an interpretation to that part of the same section of the act of 1875, which, for the purposes of statement, 'may be read as follows: ... We reserve the consideration of this provision until a case requiring it arises.'"

"[U]pon any bill in equity... shall have authority to grant injunctions, according to the course and principles of courts of equity"; and "the court is to proceed according to the course and principles of courts of equity in such cases."
"Such an action, though provided by statute, is essentially an equitable proceeding; and the rules of equity are to be followed, unless inconsistent with the statute."
Metropolitan Railroad v. District of Columbia
"such power to review is to be exerted only in the same manner and under the same regulations as theretofore prevailed"
Waterman v. Canal-Louisiana Bank & Trust Co.
“within the established equity jurisdiction of the Federal courts, which is like unto the High Court of Chancery in England at the time of the adoption of the Judiciary Act of 1789”
United States v. United States Steel Corporation

“It is clear in its denunciation of monopolies and equally clear in its direction that the courts of the Nation shall prevent and restrain them (its language is to prevent and restrain violations of the act), but the command is necessarily submissive to the conditions which may exist and the usual powers of a court of equity to adapt its remedies to those conditions.”

Mr. Justice Blatchford, speaking for the Court, admitted (p. 439), following Butterworth v. Hoe, 112 U.S. 50, 61, that the proceeding by bill in equity, under 4915 "intends a suit according to the ordinary course of equity practice and procedure, and is not a technical appeal from the Patent Office, nor confined to the case as made in the record of that office, but is prepared and heard upon all competent evidence adduced and upon the whole merits,"
Louisville Joint Stock Land Bank v. Radford

Harkelrode, 284 U.S. 225, 227, authorized the court to direct ... a power which "had long been exercised by federal courts sitting in equity when ordering sales by receivers or on foreclosure." ... By the settled practice, a sale free of liens will not be ordered by the bankruptcy court if it appears that the amount of the encumbrance exceeds the value of the property.
Atlas Life Insurance v. W. I. Southern, Inc.

The "jurisdiction" thus conferred on the federal courts to entertain suits in equity is an authority to administer in equity suits the principles of the system of judicial remedies which had been devised and was being administered by the English Court of Chancery at the time of the separation of the two countries.

"Sec. 16 of the Clayton Act provides for relief by injunction when and under the same conditions and principles as injunc-tive relief against threatened conduct that will cause loss or damage is granted by courts of equity."
"This historical meaning of bail, familiar even to laymen, must infuse our interpretation of the words of a Congress of whom, in fact, a majority were lawyers."
"If more men are sent back to work than are necessary to fill the defense needs of the country, other objectives are being served than those specified in the statute."

“In situations no more clouded with doubt than the present one we have refused to read a statutory authority to issue a decree as a command to do it. Hecht Co. v. Bowles… We there said, ‘A grant of jurisdiction to issue compliance orders hardly suggests an absolute duty to do so under any and all circumstances.’”

"It was left up to the court to decree the appropriate relief after a full hearing and if a sale was in order to fix the manner, time and condition of the same. These are details the Congress appropriately and traditionally leaves to courts."

“Discretion is implicit in the statutory command that the judge, after granting the writ and holding a hearing of appropriate scope, dispose of the matter as law and justice require, 28 U. S. C. 2243;”
United States v. First National City Bank

"The statute authorizing courts to render such decrees as may be \"necessary or appropriate for the enforcement of the internal revenue laws\" clearly intends that courts use only their traditional equity powers to that end."
"Discretion is implicit in the statutory command that the judge . . . 'dispose of the matter as law and justice require,' 28 U. S. C. 2243"
Zenith Radio Corp. v. Hazeltine Research, Inc.
"16 of the Clayton Act, 15 U. S. C. 26, ... invokes traditional principles of equity"
Johnson v. Railway Express Agency, Inc.

“It is well settled that when federal courts sit to enforce federal rights, they have an obligation to apply federal equity principles: When Congress leaves to the federal courts the formulation of remedial details, it can hardly expect them to break with historic principles of equity in the enforcement of federally-created equitable rights.”
United States v. Citizens & Southern National Bank

“We believe Congress intended the statutory proceedings before the [Federal Reserve] Board to be the sole means by which questions as to the organization or operation of a new bank by a bank holding company may be tested.”

"when and under the same conditions and principles as injunctive relief against threatened conduct that will cause loss or damage is granted by courts of equity, under the rules governing such proceedings"

“We do not believe that such a major departure from that long tradition as is here proposed should be lightly implied. ... [I]f Congress desired to make such an abrupt departure from traditional equity practice as is suggested, it would have made its desire plain.”
“A 7403 proceeding is by its nature a proceeding in equity,37 and judicial sales in general have traditionally *709been accompanied by at least a limited degree of judicial discretion.38”
Federal Trade Commission v. Grolier Inc.

“Thus, nothing in either FOIA or our decisions construing it authorizes us to define the coverage of the work-product doctrine under Exemption 5 differently from the definition of its coverage that would obtain under Rule 26(b)(3) in an ordinary lawsuit.”
United States v. Parcel of Rumson, NJ, Land
“the relation-back principle recited in 881(h) is the familiar, traditional one”
Grupo Mexicano De Desarrollo, S. A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc.

"The Judiciary Act of 1789 conferred on the federal courts jurisdiction over 'all suits . . . in equity.' ... We have long held that '[t]he `jurisdiction' thus conferred . . . is an authority to administer in equity suits the principles of the system of judicial remedies which had been devised and was being administered by the English Court of Chancery at the time of the separation of the two countries.'"
Great-West Life & Annuity Insurance v. Knudson

"[I]njunction is inherently an equitable remedy ... and statutory reference to that remedy must, absent other indication, be deemed to contain the limitations upon its availability that equity typically imposes."
Ebay Inc. v. Mercexchange, L. L. C.
"Both the terms of the Patent Act and the traditional view of injunctive relief accept that the existence of a right to exclude does not dictate the remedy for a violation of that right."
Ebay Inc. v. Mercexchange, L. L. C.

“injunctive relief may issue only in accordance with the principles of equity” ... “this Court has consistently rejected invitations to replace traditional equitable considerations with a rule that an injunction automatically follows” ... “its analysis cannot be squared with the principles of equity adopted by Congress.”
Ebay Inc. v. Mercexchange, L. L. C.

“Section 283 provides that ‘[t]he several courts having jurisdiction of cases under this title may grant injunctions in accordance with the principles of equity …’ … ‘We hold only that the decision whether to grant or deny injunctive relief rests within the equitable discretion of the district courts …’”
Sereboff v. Mid Atlantic Medical Services, Inc.
"In Mertens v. Hewitt Associates, 508 U. S. 248 (1993), we construed the provision to authorize only 'those categories of relief that were typically available in equity'"

"We have interpreted the term appropriate equitable relief in 502(a)(3) as referring to those categories of relief that, traditionally speaking (i. e., prior to the merger of law and equity), were typically available in equity."

“a litigant in a 35 U. S. C. 145 proceeding is permitted to introduce evidence not presented to the Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) according to the ordinary course of equity practice and procedure.”
Montanile v. Board of Trustees of Nat. Elevator Industry Health Benefit Plan

"Our cases explain that the term 'equitable relief' in 502(a)(3) is limited to 'those categories of relief that were typically available in equity' during the days of the divided bench (meaning, the period before 1938 when courts of law and equity were separate)."

"This Court has never treated general statutory grants of equitable authority as giving federal courts a freewheeling power to fashion new forms of equitable remedies. Rather, it has read such statutes as constrained by the body of law which had been transplanted to this country from the English Court of Chancery in 1789."
"statutory reference[s]" to a remedy grounded in equity "must, absent other indication, be deemed to contain the limitations upon its availability that equity typically imposes."

"even if Congress employed \"disgorgement\" as a shorthand to cross-reference the relief permitted by 78u(d)(5), it did not silently rewrite the scope of what the SEC could recover in a way that would contravene limitations embedded in the statute."
AMG Capital Management, LLC v. FTC

“we have held … that a provisions grant of an injunction or other equitable powers does not automatically authorize a court to provide monetary relief. Rather, we have said, the scope of equitable relief that a provision authorizes remains a question of interpretation in each case.”
